vignette:
Bounleua sits stiffly in the chair, his plumber's work-worn hands resting on his knees. At sixty-nine, his body is a map of a long, physical life, but the deepest aches are not in his joints. The trouble began over forty years ago, in a re-education camp in his native Laos, but it lives today in the basements and crawlspaces of suburban America. Last week, a client reached suddenly for a wrench just behind him, and Bounleua had flinched so violently he knocked over a bucket of fittings, his heart hammering against his ribs as if trying to escape. The client, a kind man, had apologized for startling him, but Bounleua could only nod, a cold sweat breaking out on his brow. For him, any sudden movement from another person, especially a man, is not a surprise; it is a direct and immediate threat, a prelude to a blow he has been bracing for since he was a young man.

The traumatic memories are not a coherent story he can recall, but a series of sensory fragments that play on a loop. He calls it "the film." There is the damp, earthy smell of the hut, the glint in a guard's eye, the constant, grinding ache in his neck from being forced to kneel with his head bowed for hours. When these images surface, a wave of nausea rises from his stomach, the same sickening lurch he felt when they were given spoiled rice. He has learned to fight it by detaching, by focusing with laser intensity on the immediate physical world. He will stare at the threads on a PVC pipe, feeling the grit under his calloused thumbs, forcing his mind into the here-and-now until the film flickers and fades. He knows what happened, but when he tries to speak of it, the words scatter. He once attempted to explain to his wife, Somsri, but found himself stammering, losing the thread, the sequence of events tangling into an incomprehensible knot of fear. Now he just says he can't find the words, a silence she has learned to respect but which has carved a hollow space between them.

This internal battle dictates the shape of his days. Before Bounleua even brings his toolbox into a client's home, he does a silent, swift calculation, mapping the exits. He will always position himself to face the door, never allowing anyone to stand behind him. This vigilance does not end when he clocks out. At home, a place he has lived for thirty years, he still feels perpetually on guard, checking the locks twice and always sitting in the chair that faces the entrance to the room. Working with male clients is a particular strain. If he has to be alone in a house with a man, a low-level hum of anxiety starts, and if there are two or more men, the tension becomes a physical presence, tightening his shoulders and bringing on the familiar, dull pain in his neck. That pain has become more than just a physical ailment; it is a somatic alarm bell. The moment he feels that specific ache, the film starts rolling, and he is back in the camp, a young man again, paralyzed by fear.

Over the years, his family has learned his unspoken rules. They know not to approach him from behind. Somsri knows that during a certain week in April, he will be quiet and withdrawn, and she no longer asks why. He avoids the date as if it were a physical place, a contaminated zone on the calendar that he must navigate around. But recently, the strategies have started to fail. The neck pain is more constant, a persistent trigger he cannot avoid. The physical reactivity is more pronounced, leaving him shaky and exhausted after a simple service call. It was the incident with the wrench, the sheer, uncontrolled panic in his own body, that finally brought him to seek help. He is afraid he is losing the battle, that one day the film will start and he won't be able to turn it off. He cannot explain his past to his wife, but he hopes, with a quiet desperation, that he might finally find the words for a stranger.
